title: Blue Hour and Radiators
premise: Beatrix Lockridge has spent three years mailing unsent confessions to the charred address of Halcyon House, where her brother Elias died in a fire the town called an accident and she privately calls a verdict. When a late-night radio DJ plays a song Elias wrote and never recorded — a melody she alone has heard — Beatrix realizes someone alive holds his lost notebook, and she hunts the signal through pawnshops, prison chaplains, and a demolition crew racing toward the house's ruins. The notebook's final page holds one untranslated sentence in their invented childhood cipher, the sentence she has been almost-saying for three years. In the house's last standing room, on the morning the wrecking ball arrives, Beatrix translates it aloud — 'I know what you did, and I stayed anyway' — choosing truth over the law's version of justice, and finally lets the house, and the sentence, go.
about_author: Cyrus Fairweather is the pen name of a former small-town obituary writer who spent a decade collecting the letters people never mailed. He writes from a rented room above a defunct radio station, where he claims the static still talks back.

chapters.title: The Address That Burned
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She writes her 214th postcard to Halcyon House, burned three years ago, and mails it anyway. Establish her ritual, her job at a stationery shop, and her refusal to say what she means. Beat: numb devotion.

chapters.title: Static at 2 A.M.
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Sleepless, she hears a late-night radio DJ play a song Elias wrote in their teens and never recorded. Her hands go cold. Beat: the impossible made audible.

chapters.title: Cipher for Beginners
chapters.summary: Flashback, Beatrix's POV. Childhood at Halcyon House: Elias invents a two-person cipher, and Beatrix learns that some sentences are only safe when translated. Beat: tender complicity.

chapters.title: The DJ Who Plays Ghosts
chapters.summary: Beatrix tracks the broadcast to a community station and confronts Marisol Vega, the DJ, who plays 'songs people swear don't exist.' Marisol admits a man left her a cassette, no name. Beat: first thread pulled.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The county posts a demolition order on Halcyon House: forty days. The town celebrates; Beatrix reads it as a deadline on her silence. Beat: the clock starts.

chapters.title: What the Fire Report Says
chapters.summary: Beatrix requests the official fire file and finds it sanitized — origin 'undetermined,' a witness statement missing. Justice, she sees, was never interested in the truth. Beat: quiet outrage.

chapters.title: Aunt Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Beatrix visits Aunt Odile, who inherited the house and wants it gone. Odile reveals Elias had been recording in the attic the week he died — on equipment that vanished. Beat: the theft within the tragedy.

chapters.title: The Pawnshop Man
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Following the missing recorder, she finds a pawnbroker who bought it from a man with a prison tattoo and a limp — and who kept one cassette for himself. Beat: the trail warms.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She drafts a postcard that finally says the thing and burns it instead. Interweave the untranslated cipher sentence, which she can read but not speak. Beat: self-betrayal.

chapters.title: Marisol's Second Tape
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The DJ plays the ghost-song again and receives a threatening letter telling her to stop. She hides a second cassette under her booth and starts her own investigation. Beat: ally in danger.

chapters.title: The Man with the Limp
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She identifies him: Deacon Wray, a former handyman at Halcyon House, released from prison last spring for arson — a fire that wasn't theirs. Beat: suspect or scapegoat?

chapters.title: Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Beatrix visits Deacon in a halfway house. He denies setting Elias's fire but admits he took the recorder — as payment for his silence about what he saw that night. Beat: a witness bought and buried.

chapters.title: What Deacon Saw
chapters.summary: Deacon's POV, guarded and halting. He describes a car in the driveway, two voices arguing about money and 'the papers,' and someone leaving with a satchel before the flames. Beat: the accident cracks open.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. 'The papers' points to the house's deed and Elias's discovery that Aunt Odile had quietly encumbered Halcyon House against debts — motive. Beat: inheritance as crime scene.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Her show is pulled from the schedule after the threats escalate. She gives Beatrix the hidden cassette and quits on air, live. Beat: sacrifice, solidarity.

chapters.title: Side B
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, alone at night. The cassette is Elias's voice: half-finished songs, then a fight recorded through a floorboard — and a name half-caught. Beat: the dead speak.

chapters.title: The Name Under the Static
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Marisol clean the audio: the voice is Odile's. But the second voice says something that stops Beatrix cold — it sounds like herself, three years younger. Beat: vertigo.

chapters.title: What I Did That Night
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, fractured memory. She was at the house that night; she left before the fire, after an argument with Elias she has never finished remembering. Beat: the almost-said turns inward.

chapters.title: Odile Denies Everything
chapters.summary: Beatrix confronts Odile with the tape. Odile is cold, then frightened, then vicious: 'That house ate your brother long before the fire.' Beat: the family's rot surfaces.

chapters.title: Threat, Delivered
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Someone ransacks her apartment and takes the cassette and her three years of postcards. A note: 'Stop digging or be dug under.' Beat: the cost of truth made physical.

chapters.title: The Postcard Thief
chapters.summary: Beatrix suspects everyone, then realizes only one person knew where she kept the cards: the stationery shop's owner, Ruth, who has been quietly reading them for years — and who once worked for Odile. Beat: betrayal in plain sight.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. She was paid by Odile to watch Beatrix, but reading the postcards broke her; she never gave Odile the ones that mattered. She returns a bundle — including the untranslated sentence's key page. Beat: mercy from an unlikely hand.

chapters.title: The Cipher Key
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. With the key page she can finally translate the sentence — and refuses to read it, because translating it means admitting what she did that night. Beat: the door she won't open.

chapters.title: Deacon Disappears
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Deacon vanishes from the halfway house the day after Odile visits him. Marisol finds his burned notebook of testimony in a bus-station locker. Beat: the witness silenced, the evidence survives.

chapters.title: Twenty Days Left
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Halfway to demolition, she petitions the county to halt it pending investigation and is refused — the paperwork is 'in order.' Justice outside the law becomes her only road. Beat: the system closes.

chapters.title: Going Public
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Marisol broadcast the cleaned tape on a pirate signal from the old station tower. The town hears Elias's voice and the argument beneath it. Beat: the private becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: The Town Turns
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs. Neighbors who celebrated the demolition now stand at the fence; the county delays 'pending review.' Odile's lawyer circles. Beat: the tide shifts, uneasily.

chapters.title: Odile's Counterstory
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She tells her version: Elias was blackmailing her over the deed, the fire was his own doing, and Beatrix's memory is a child's invention. It's half-true, which makes it dangerous. Beat: the villain gains a face.

chapters.title: Doubt
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Odile's version lodges in her; the half-memory of that night won't resolve. She nearly signs a settlement to make it stop. Beat: the darkest hour of certainty.

chapters.title: Elias's Last Song
chapters.summary: Beatrix listens to Side B's final track — a finished song Elias never got to record, addressed 'to B.' In it, he forgives someone in advance. She weeps, and the memory begins to unlock. Beat: grace from the dead.

chapters.title: The Night, Remembered
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV, full flashback. The truth: she saw Odile leave with the satchel; Elias begged her not to tell; she ran, and the fire started minutes later. Her silence was shame, not guilt. Beat: the sentence translated at last, in the heart.

chapters.title: I Know What You Did
chapters.summary: Beatrix speaks the translated sentence aloud, alone in her apartment: 'I know what you did, and I stayed anyway.' It is addressed to the house, to Elias, to herself. Beat: the untranslatable, translated.

chapters.title: Deacon Found
chapters.summary: Marisol and Beatrix find Deacon alive, paid off and hiding. He agrees to sign his testimony if Beatrix stands beside him publicly. Beat: courage is contagious.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At the county review, she reads Deacon's testimony and her own postcards into the record — three years of almost-saying, finally said. Odile's lawyer objects; the room listens. Beat: justice outside the law, spoken inside it.

chapters.title: Odile at the Door
chapters.summary: Odile comes to Beatrix at night, not to threaten but to ask what Elias's last words to her were. Beatrix tells the truth. Odile leaves without absolution. Beat: the villain humanized, unforgiven.

chapters.title: Five Days
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. The demolition stays scheduled — the county won't reverse it — but the investigation into Odile opens. Beatrix requests one thing: to be inside when it falls. Beat: acceptance.

chapters.title: Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Beatrix, Marisol, Ruth, and Deacon gather at the house at blue hour. Beatrix plays Elias's last song on a battery radio in the empty parlor and leaves her 215th postcard on the mantel, finally legible. Beat: communion.

chapters.title: The Wrecking Ball
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. From the fence she watches Halcyon House come down, translating the sentence one last time under her breath as the walls fold. She does not look away. Beat: the climax — grief and truth in the same breath.

chapters.title: What the Rubble Keeps
chapters.summary: Weeks later. Odile is indicted; the fire report is reopened; Deacon testifies. Beatrix finds, in the rubble's edge, the attic's tin box — Elias's original notebook, the sentence in his hand, and one word added: 'Stay.' Beat: inheritance redefined.

chapters.title: Radiators
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. Winter. In a new apartment with clanking radiators, she writes her first postcard with a deliverable address — to Marisol's show, requesting a song. The DJ reads it on air: the sentence, said plainly, and the town hears. Beat: resolution — the almost-said becomes the said, and she lives with it.
